title: Torsional selection rule for the spin--orbit conversion of light
abstract: Standard Pancharatnam-Berry and linear-birefringent media convert optical spin into orbital angular momentum (OAM) through an anisotropy \emph{director}, a rank-two, headless field, and therefore obey the selection rule $Δ\ell=2q$ per unit texture charge $q$. We show that a medium with geometric \emph{torsion}, the continuum limit of a screw-dislocation array, can convert spin to OAM through the \emph{contortion} of its material connection, which enters the effective paraxial dynamics as a rank-one vector field. The resulting selection rule is $Δ\ell=q$. Its winding is fixed by geometry and symmetry, not by a Pancharatnam--Berry director, and the process conserves the screw charge $\tilde J_z=L_z+(q/2)σ_z$ while exchanging $(2-q)\hbar$ of angular momentum per converted photon with the defect lattice. Paraxial simulations confirm the rule: a circular Gaussian input develops a stable, topologically quantized $\ell=+q$ vortex in the reversed helicity, with $83\%$ conversion over three Rayleigh ranges and no fine-tuning. We propose a polarization-resolved photonic-lattice discriminator in which the slope of the measured OAM versus the independently written texture charge, one for torsion, two for birefringence, separates the two mechanisms.
summary: This paper introduces a novel mechanism where light's spin converts to orbital angular momentum via the geometric torsion of a medium, yielding a selection rule $\Delta\ell=q$. This contrasts sharply with the established Pancharatnam–Berry rule ($\Delta\ell=2q$). The authors provide theoretical derivations and simulation results, culminating in a proposal for an experiment that can directly measure this topological difference.
main_problem: The paper aims to distinguish between two mechanisms for converting light's spin angular momentum (SAM) into orbital angular momentum (OAM): the standard Pancharatnam–Berry mechanism and a novel process mediated by geometric torsion.
main_result: Torsion-mediated conversion follows a selection rule $\Delta\ell=q$, which is distinct from the PB rule ($\Delta\ell=2q$), allowing for experimental discrimination using polarization-resolved measurements.
method: The authors use theoretical modeling (effective paraxial Maxwell equations) combined with numerical simulations and propose an experimental discriminator setup.
model_or_system: The system involves light propagating through a material exhibiting geometric torsion, modeled as a continuum of screw dislocations. The coupling is described by an effective Hamiltonian involving the contortion tensor, leading to a rank-one field interaction.
key_observables: The primary observables are the resulting OAM ($\ell$) versus the written texture charge ($q$), which should yield slopes of 1 (torsional) or 2 (PB).
important_parameters: Key parameters include the topological charges $q$ and the coupling strengths $\Gamma(r)$ and $\kappa(r)$. The conversion efficiency is shown to saturate at high values.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the physical signatures, such as torque conservation ($	ilde{J}_z$) and the functional dependence of OAM on $q$, are distinct enough to separate the two coupling mechanisms.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares winding patterns for rank-2 (PB) vs. rank-1 (torsional). Figure 2 shows simulated vortex generation ($\ell=+1$ spiral) with high efficiency. Figure 3 proposes an experiment showing non-overlapping OAM spectra for $\Delta\ell=q$ versus $\Delta\ell=2q$.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical difference between PB coupling (rank-two director, $\Delta\ell=2q$) and torsional coupling (rank-one contortion, $\Delta\ell=q$). It then presents simulations confirming the selection rule and proposes a concrete experimental setup using lattice writing to measure this distinction.
why_interesting: This work bridges geometric optics with condensed matter topology by showing how material defects (torsion) can provide an alternative, quantifiable mechanism for light-matter interaction that is fundamentally different from standard Berry phase effects.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. The selection rule distinguishes the rank of the me- diating field. (a) A Pancharatnam–Berry element couples the circular components through a rank-two director texture of charge q; the coupling winds as e±i2qφ. (b) A torsional (Riemann–Cartan) medium couples them through the rank- one contortion vector, which winds as e±iqφ. (c),(d) Simu- lated OAM spectra of the converted beam E−for the same texture charge q = 1 and identical coupling magnitude: the sideband appears at ℓ= +2 (PB) versus ℓ= +1 (torsional).

FIG. 2. Torsional vortex generation (q = 1). (a) Phase of the converted field at z = 25 w0: a stable, charge-n=+1 spiral. (b) Conversion η = P−and mean OAM versus propagation distance; both saturate at 0.83. (c) Final conversion versus holonomy strength κ0: a broad maximum (η ≃0.85) with no fine-tuning; in every run the charge is quantized at n = +1. Full sweeps in (κ0, Γ0), paraxial parameter k0 = 8–64, and grid refinement are given in the SM [27].

(a) A circularly polarized Gaussian traverses a femtosecond-written lattice with a screw- dislocation texture of charge q (L ≃5 mm at δn ∼10−3); the output is helicity-sorted and its OAM measured. (b) Predicted OAM of the converted beam versus texture charge, from full simulations of Eq.
